name: mediaconch
desc: Conformance checker and technical metadata reporter
why: Checks media files against archival conformance policies, a real look into file format internals if you dig in.

brief.what_it_is: MediaConch is an open source toolset that checks preservation-level audiovisual files against conformance policies. Its parts are an implementation checker, a policy checker, a reporter, and a fixer. It targets Matroska, LPCM and FFV1 files, and it can be run from the command line, a graphical user interface, or a web interface. The homepage describes an adaptable application program interface for detailed individual and batch-level conformance checking. The input is media files, and the output is conformance and technical reports.
brief.why_it_exists: It exists to improve standardization and validation of preservation-level audiovisual files in memory institutions, and to help keep Matroska, LPCM and FFV1 viable as recommended digital preservation formats. The README frames it as a way to validate, assess and find solutions to repair files in collections.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the implementation checker, policy checker, reporter and fixer work together to validate files. The repository list says the analysis engine is MediaInfoLib, extended with Matroska and FFV1 tests, and that XSD schemas for MediaConch, MediaInfo and MediaTrace live in a separate repository. The README does not describe the internals beyond this.
brief.install_notes: Downloads are offered for Windows, macOS, Debian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint, Raspbian, RedHat Enterprise Linux, CentOS, Fedora, openSUSE, ArchLinux, Flatpak, Snap, AppImage, AWS Lambda, and JavaScript, plus other systems. The homepage lists Version 25.04 and says other versions are available. Monthly releases and nightly builds are on the project's download page. No account, runtime or configuration steps were described in the pages I read. The homepage also offers MediaConchOnline, which needs no installation.
brief.standout: It is built by the MediaArea team, which also made MediaInfo, and it is aimed at archival preservation rather than general media inspection. It also contributes to the standardization of Matroska and FFV1 themselves, and it keeps a public research corpus (MediaConch_MKVSurvey) and sample files for testing.
brief.status: Probably maintained. The homepage shows Version 25.04 and offers nightly builds, and the README commits to monthly releases. I did not find a last-commit or release date, so I cannot confirm recency.
brief.caveats: Licensing is inconsistent across the pages I read. The homepage says all MediaArea software is under BSD-2-Clause. The GitHub README says software developed under the PREFORMA project is GPLv3-or-later or MPLv2-or-later. The README also says the design-phase documentation lives in the main repository. The README's third-party licence list includes Qt, which is optional for the GUI. The README mentions a Microsoft proprietary library for Windows builds. The README says test-file coverage is still being built, so it is not a complete corpus yet. Build instructions and platform details beyond the download list were not in the pages I read.
quotes: MediaConch is an extensible, open source software project consisting of an implementation checker, policy checker, reporter, and fixer that targets preservation-level audiovisual files
With a project focus dedicated to furthering the longevity of Matroska, Linear Pulse Code Modulation (LPCM) and FF Video Codec 1 (FFV1) as recommended digital preservation audiovisual formats
You can also use MediaConchOnline to test MediaConch without installing any software on your computer.

judge.reason: A specialized tool for testing audiovisual files against preservation policies exposes the standards and internals behind formats most developers never inspect.

entry.title: MediaConch
entry.tldr: A conformance checker for archival video and audio files that tells you whether a Matroska, FFV1 or LPCM file really follows its spec.
entry.deeper_look:
MediaConch checks preservation-level audiovisual files against rules. It has four parts: an implementation checker (does the file follow the format spec?), a policy checker (does it meet the rules your institution set?), a reporter, and a fixer. It targets Matroska, LPCM and FFV1, and it runs from the command line, a GUI, or a web interface. The output is conformance and technical reports.

It exists for memory institutions such as archives and libraries, which need to know that the files in their collections are valid and will stay readable. The project's stated aim is "furthering the longevity of Matroska, Linear Pulse Code Modulation (LPCM) and FF Video Codec 1 (FFV1) as recommended digital preservation audiovisual formats." The README frames it as a way to validate files, assess them, and find ways to repair them.

The idea underneath is that a file that plays is not the same as a file that is correct. Container formats leave room for malformed structures, odd choices and quiet corruption, and a long-term archive cannot rely on whichever player happens to forgive them. Checking a file against a spec and a written policy is a way to see how a media container is put together. The analysis engine is MediaInfoLib, extended with Matroska and FFV1 tests.

It comes from MediaArea, the team behind MediaInfo. They also contribute to the standardization of Matroska and FFV1 themselves, and they keep a public research corpus (MediaConch_MKVSurvey) and sample files for testing.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the command-line options, which is the place to start since the brief lists no example commands.

entry.whats_unique: It is aimed at archival preservation rather than general media inspection, and its authors help shape the Matroska and FFV1 standards it checks against.
entry.caveats: The pages disagree on licensing (BSD-2-Clause on the homepage, GPLv3 or MPLv2 terms in the README), and the README says test-file coverage is still being built.
